title: Glory Theme
summary: In Exodus 3, Moses encounters God in fire at the bush that is not consumed; later, the cloud and glory fill the tabernacle, and in 1 Kings 8 the temple is filled as well. John says the Word became flesh and that witnesses saw his glory. Revelation 21 shifts the image to God dwelling with humanity. These scenes link glory with God’s presence, but the texts show that presence in different ways: a call, a sanctuary, a person, and a promised dwelling.
historical_context: The passages follow a sequence in Israel’s story and later Christian texts. Exodus 3 places Moses’ call at Horeb; Exodus 40 describes the completed tabernacle filled by the cloud and glory. At the dedication of Solomon’s temple, 1 Kings 8 describes the cloud filling the house. John 1 speaks of the Word becoming flesh, while Revelation 21 pictures God dwelling with humanity in the renewed world. The last passage develops the theme of divine dwelling rather than repeating the earlier sanctuary scene.
literary_context: The theme appears through different literary forms. Exodus 3 narrates a call and the burning bush; Exodus 40 closes the tabernacle instructions with the cloud covering the tent and God’s glory filling it. First Kings 8 recounts a similar filling at the temple’s dedication. John 1 uses a compact theological introduction to connect the Word’s presence among people with glory seen by witnesses. Revelation 21 uses apocalyptic vision to portray God dwelling with humanity. Their shared language invites a canonical connection without making each scene identical.
covenantal_significance: These passages portray God’s presence as a gift that accompanies and directs the people: God calls Moses, fills the sanctuary, and is associated with the temple’s dedication. John locates the presence-and-glory theme in the Word made flesh; Revelation looks toward God dwelling with humanity. The movement from sanctuary to promised dwelling deepens the theme while preserving the distinct claims of each passage.
canonical_role: Glory Theme serves as a thematic anchor, connecting repeated biblical patterns, key passages, and related theological concepts across the canon.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Glory Theme in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
